subtopic: Using AI tools inside a team
subtype: Approach: sharing prompts and lessons in a team log [Action]
passage: Sit down, Yusuf. You asked how our team got good with these AI tools. Honestly, it wasn't the clever ones among us. When we started, three people knew the tricks and everyone else kept guessing. So I began a shared page. Whenever someone found a request that worked, they pasted it in with one line on why; whenever one failed, they pasted that too, and what went wrong. Every Friday afternoon, before chai, we read the page together for twenty minutes. Nobody was laughed at for a failure. Within two months, people who hadn't dared before were adding entries, and the same mistake stopped repeating. I'm Harish, and if you take one thing from me: skill kept in one head leaves when that person does.

qa.q: When did the team read the shared page together?
qa.a: They read it every Friday afternoon, before chai, for twenty minutes.

qa.q: What did Harish want when starting the shared page?
qa.a: Harish wanted skill to spread across the team instead of staying with three people, worried that it would leave with them.

qa.q: Which choice inside the story helped quiet members start adding entries, and why?
qa.a: Not laughing at failures helped, since it made it safe for people who had not dared before to share what went wrong.

qa.q: How might a quiet team member have felt before the page existed?
qa.a: They were probably unsure and a little left out, guessing while three colleagues seemed to know the tricks.

grounding: Shows team members noting prompts that worked and failed and reviewing them on Fridays so skill grows across the team.

subtopic: Using AI tools inside a team
subtype: Approach: sharing prompts and lessons in a team log [Action]
passage:
Keerthana's team of five was split between Chennai and Gangtok, and the video calls kept freezing in the monsoon. Everyone was using the AI assistant differently, and the same mistakes kept repeating. Tenzin had spent two hours on a prompt that Keerthana had already cracked the week before.
So she started a shared page called 'Prompt log'. Three columns: what I asked, what worked, what went wrong. On Monday she added the first entries herself: a prompt that wrote good test cases, and one that confidently invented a library function that doesn't exist.
By the second Friday there were twenty-three entries. They went through them on a call, cameras off to save bandwidth. Tenzin read out his trick for getting clear commit messages. Two people copied it on the spot.

qa.q: What were the three columns on the page?
qa.a: What I asked, what worked, what went wrong.

qa.q: How might Tenzin have felt learning that Keerthana had already cracked the prompt?
qa.a: Tenzin was probably frustrated at the wasted two hours, which shows why a shared log was needed.

qa.q: What else could the team do to keep the log useful as it grows?
qa.a: They could tag entries by task and remove outdated prompts each month, so the best ones stay easy to find.

qa.q: How does the log look to the teammates who copied Tenzin's trick?
qa.a: They gain a skill in minutes that took Tenzin effort to find, so the log spreads learning across the team.

grounding: It shows a team noting prompts that worked and failures in a shared log and going through them on Fridays so skills spread across the team.

subtopic: Using AI tools inside a team
subtype: Approach: sharing prompts and lessons in a team log [Action]
passage:
In the small analytics office above a bank in Lucknow, only two people really knew how to get good work out of the AI tools: Saurabh and one intern. Everyone else asked them. Ujjwal, the newest analyst, asked Saurabh four times in one morning.
That afternoon Saurabh opened a shared notebook and titled it 'What worked, what didn't'. He wrote the first entry: the exact prompt he used to clean messy survey data, and underneath, a failure: the tool had once merged two different districts with similar names. He asked everyone to add one entry a week.
On Fridays at four, the team spent twenty minutes reading the new entries aloud. By the end of the month, Ujjwal had written the entry the others used most: a prompt to explain a chart in plain Hindi for field staff.

qa.q: When did the team read the new entries?
qa.a: On Fridays at four, for twenty minutes.

qa.q: How might Ujjwal have felt asking Saurabh four times in one morning?
qa.a: Ujjwal probably felt awkward and dependent, eager to learn but embarrassed to keep asking.

qa.q: Why was including a failure in the first entry a good choice?
qa.a: It showed that mistakes belong in the notebook too, so others learn what to watch for, like mixed-up districts.

qa.q: How might Saurabh's work change as the notebook grows?
qa.a: Saurabh gets fewer interruptions, and the team's skills no longer depend on two people.

grounding: It shows a team keeping a shared log of prompts that worked and failed and reading it together on Fridays, so skills grow beyond a few people.
